Description:

This mixed-media work by Lennart Olausson brings together soft, organic forms with a sharply constructed abstract framework. A large, coiling, almost cloud-like form occupies the centre of the composition, rendered in subtle shades of grey and black and set against blocks of deep crimson and black. The contrast between the cloud-like form and the rigid geometry surrounding it gives the work a dreamlike, slightly enigmatic quality, characteristic of Olausson’s interest in combining recognisable imagery with abstraction and ambiguity.

Lennart Olausson made his gallery debut at Galleri Doktor Glas in Stockholm in 1968, followed by an exhibition at Galerie Belle in Västerås the following year. Educated at Konstfack and the Royal Institute of Art in Stockholm, Olausson developed a distinctive visual language combining precise observation, surreal elements and art-historical references. His work is represented in major Swedish collections including Moderna Museet and the Nationalmuseum.

Signed Lennart Olausson

Description:

This precise pencil drawing, titled Plangeometri (Plane Geometry) reflects Gösta Adrian-Nilsson’s intense engagement with geometric abstraction and Constructivism. Composed of interlocking planes, lines and measured forms, it belongs to a period in which GAN increasingly moved towards a more structured and disciplined visual language, following his earlier explorations of Cubism, Futurism and Expressionism.

Gösta Adrian-Nilsson (1884–1965), universally known as GAN, was one of the pioneers of Swedish modernism. His encounters with the European avant-garde during periods in Berlin and Paris were instrumental in the development of his highly individual style, which brought together Cubism, Futurism, Constructivism and Expressionism. His work from the late 1920s and early 1930s is particularly important for its exploration of geometry, movement and the relationship between abstract form and architectural space.

On display at our Stockholm gallery
Description:

Rune Hagberg (1924 - 2015) was a self-taught pupil of Zen Buddhism who explored silence and introspection within his work.

Born in Uppsala, Sweden, Hagberg became heavily influenced by Eastern calligraphy throughout his life – and developed a spontaneous sign painting style with a strong concentration on a select amount of characters rooted in Zen Buddhism. His informal meditative practice found its place between concretism and expressionism which was widespread in the 1950s. Later in his life, these symbols would be bound into reels and tied together with string - white, ascetic, and secretive within their frames.

Eventually, Hagberg's practice came to focus on a gradual loosening of the picture surface, a kind of elimination of the sheet of paper, as if to approach the idea of nothingness. This exploration later found expression in sculptural objects.

His oeuvre of ink painting turned him into a public figure in Sweden – hosting a long series of exhibitions, most notably at Moderna Museet in Malmö and Norrköping Art Museum. He also exhibited abroad in Japan in 1955 alongside a group of Eastern painters and calligraphers.

Signed

description:
Reference number: 8514 / SL-29

Material:

Book covers on linen canvas applied on board.

Measurements:
H: 120 cm / 3' 11 3/4"
L: 90 cm / 2' 11 7/16"
On display at our London gallery
Description:

This collage, titled Bortom Polcirkeln (Beyond the Arctic Circle), was created by David Svensson and forms part of his Coverings series. The work is composed from the covers and endpapers of old books, carefully arranged into a vertical, geometric composition that balances symmetry, surface, and subtle tonal variation. Removed from their original function, the book covers are transformed into a sculptural form.

Svensson began working with discarded books in the late 2000s, initially drawn to handwritten dedications and personal notes. Over time, his focus shifted toward the physical structure of the book itself, particularly the cover as an object bearing memory without explicit narrative. The absence of text becomes a central feature, allowing material, colour, and proportion to carry meaning. Like many works in the series, the composition has been described as resembling a map or a poetic diagram of unknown territory.

David Svensson, born in 1973, was educated at Malmö Art Academy, the Royal Institute of Art in Stockholm, and the National Academy of Fine Arts in Oslo. His work has been widely exhibited in Sweden and internationally, and is represented in several public collections.

description:

With frame
134 x 85 cm / 4' 4 3/4" x 2' 9 1/2"
Description:

Komposition I from 1959 is a rigorous and concentrated work from Ole Schwalbe’s formative years within Danish Constructivism. Built from sharply defined rectangular fields, the composition balances black, white, and red in a tightly controlled arrangement.

During the late 1950s, Schwalbe deliberately reduced his use of colour to these three tones. This limitation allowed Schwalbe to focus fully on relationships between form, colour, and spatial rhythm.

Ole Schwalbe was a central figure in the second generation of Danish Constructivists, associated with the Linien group and the movement they termed concrete realism. Although trained as a lithographer, he was largely self-taught as a painter and approached painting as an autonomous visual system, free from representation.

Signed

Description:

This 1962 oil painting, titled ‘Homage à Tatlin III’, is an exceptional work by Danish modernist painter Ole Schwalbe. Paying tribute to Russian constructivist Vladimir Tatlin, Schwalbe explores geometric abstraction through bold shapes and striking colour fields. The canvas features a minimalist composition in varying shades of deep blue, accented by precise black lines and rounded forms, reflecting the influence of constructivist ideals.

The painting is divided into distinct sections, with sharp rectangles and lines anchoring the composition on the left, contrasted by the curved shapes to the right. The careful balance of flat planes and subtle texture speaks to Schwalbe’s ability to harmonize opposing forces within his work, a hallmark of his geometric abstract style.

This abstract painting reflects the mature language developed by Curt Fors. His career is marked by a gradual transition from figurative beginnings to a distinctive abstract practice focused on form, tone and spatial relationships.

Fors has described his preference for abstract painting earlier as such: “Abstract painting is the term...freer than concrete painting'', he says. ''More feeling, more French culture. The details should be just as exciting the closer you get to the work''.

Born in 1935, Curt Fors is an established Swedish visual artist, photographer, and sculptor. After early figurative work, he moved decisively toward abstraction, developing a distinctive and disciplined visual language. Having lived and worked in Malmö, Stockholm, and Paris, his work is represented in major public collections, including the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm..

Working in a purely geometric, non-figurative style, Sven Hansson was a Swedish painter who is now represented in various collections, including the Moderna Museet in Stockholm. His gouache, oil, and relief pieces throughout the 1970s to late 90s are quietly expressive forms of contemporary art, on occasion using vibrant colour, many examples are executed in pure white and therefore rely on natural light and the resulting shadows.

Hansson pursued his artistic education at Valand's Art School in Gothenburg and further honed his skills under the mentorship of André Lhote at Académie André Lhote in Paris. Description:

This pair of wall reliefs, titled Skylight, was created by Irene Fortuyn in collaboration with Robert O’Brien as part of their shared exploration of art integrated into everyday environments.

Executed as circular reliefs, the surfaces evoke a sense of depth and atmosphere, blurring the boundary between painting and object. The imagery recalls a view upward, as if through an opening or window, bringing an impression of the outdoors into the room. This approach reflects Fortuyn and O’Brien’s long-standing interest in dissolving distinctions between inside and outside, nature and built environment, and between art and daily life.

Irene Fortuyn’s practice spans sculpture, landscape-related works, and spatial installations, often extending beyond gallery settings into parks and public or domestic contexts. Together with Robert O’Brien, she challenged conventional ideas of where art belongs, insisting that space, setting, and human interaction are fundamental to meaning.

Description:

This painting belongs to the Kabala series created during the 1980s by the Swedish-American artist Siri Berg. Executed on canvas mounted on stretched linen, the work is composed of softly intersecting geometric planes rendered in muted, translucent tones.

The Kabala series was developed in close dialogue with Jewish mysticism, particularly the concept of the ten Sefirot, understood as stages or manifestations of the divine. Berg translated these metaphysical ideas into visual form through gradual colour transitions from darker to lighter tones, using harmony and balance to suggest spiritual progression and the reconciliation of opposing forces.

Siri Berg was born in Stockholm in 1921 and emigrated to the United States at the age of nineteen. Her lifelong engagement with colour was shaped by her studies with Zita Querido in New York, a former student and associate of Hans Hofmann. Over several decades, Berg developed a highly personal visual language grounded in colour theory, perception, and transcendence. Her work is represented in major institutional collections, including the Guggenheim Museum in New York and the Moderna Museet in Stockholm, underscoring her significance within postwar abstract and colour-based art.

This work created by Lars Englund in 1988, exemplifies his distinctive approach to relief-based abstraction. Composed as a shallow, wall-mounted structure, the piece brings together drawing, sculpture, and object, with small modular elements forming a gently expanding triangular configuration. Englund’s practice developed from the early 1960s onward, when he began working with materials associated with modern industry, including plastics, rubber, and later carbon fibre.

Trained under Vilhelm Bjerke-Petersen and later Fernand Léger, Englund maintained a strict constructivist foundation throughout his career, while continuously reworking a limited set of forms into new spatial relationships. His reliefs and sculptures are often built from a single basic unit that is extended, mirrored, or combined into evolving configurations, a method that lends his work a sense of continuity and internal logic. Lars Englund is regarded as one of the most formally rigorous figures in Swedish twentieth-century art. His work has been exhibited internationally, and he represented Sweden at several major biennales.

From the 1960s onward, Englund was among the first Swedish artists to adopt modern industrial materials such as plastics, rubber, concrete, and later carbon fibre. By working with materials associated with everyday production rather than traditional fine art, he sought to reveal their aesthetic potential and to question hierarchies between the ordinary and the refined.

This paired set of relief paintings, titled Around Malevitch and created in 1976 by Poul Pedersen, forms a quiet yet incisive meditation on modernist legacy and perception. Executed in a restrained white-on-white palette, each work consists of subtly tilted geometric elements mounted within shallow frames.

The series takes its point of departure from the ideas of Kazimir Malevich and Suprematism, particularly the pursuit of pure, non-representational expression through simple geometric forms. Pedersen was a central figure in the Aarhus avant-garde of the 1960s, known for a conceptual practice that probes how meaning is constructed through symbols, systems and art history itself. This unique woven painting was created in 2002 by David Svensson. Rather than applying paint to a traditional support, Svensson builds the image from the material itself. Thin streams of liquid acrylic are poured onto plastic surfaces and left to cure, after which the dried paint is cut into narrow strips and interlaced using a plain-weave technique. David Svensson, born in 1973, was educated at Malmö Art Academy, the Royal Institute of Art in Stockholm, and the National Academy of Fine Arts in Oslo. His practice spans painting, sculpture, and large-scale public installations, and his work is represented in several major collections. Alongside his studio work, he is widely known for technically complex public commissions, including permanent light installations in urban environments across Sweden.

This abstract painting by Albert Johansson, executed in oil on board during the 1960s, demonstrates the artist’s exploration of geometric form and spatial tension. Bold black shapes intersect with fields of red and white, while fine linear contours frame and guide the composition.

A defining element of Johansson’s work is the use of lines that appear to “cut” across the surface of the painting. These directional lines divide the composition into shifting planes, producing a sense of expansion beyond the physical limits of the image. This approach aligns Johansson with the ideas of concrete art and reflects the influence of the Swedish artist Olle Baertling, whose exploration of infinite space through angular structures shaped much of the period’s abstract language.

Albert Johansson (1926–1998) studied at Isaac Grünewald’s painting school before continuing his education at the Modern Art School in Stockholm. Although his earliest works were influenced by Surrealism, he soon moved toward a non-figurative mode of expression. Johansson later became known for his rigorous abstract compositions, where line, colour and geometry interact to create structured yet visually expansive works.
